column2: And for a record in Portuguese, Catalan, English, Russian, Ukrainian, Hebrew, Yiddish, Armenian or Arabic (graves included)?
column3: The same “📜 Help reading old records”: choose the language badge (“＋ other languages” to see them all). For each: the words of birth, marriage and death, the months, numbers and ages, occupations, kinship, translated formulas and a model exercise (example people) corrected word by word. English also has the census abbreviations (Ag. Lab., Unm., Do) and those of the Ellis Island lists (S.I., L.P.C.). For Russian, Ukrainian, Hebrew, Yiddish, Armenian and Arabic, you can search and answer in Latin letters: “krestianin”, “tichri”, “geshtorbn”, “krikor”, “marhoum”. Russian before 1918 (ѣ, ъ, і, ѳ) is explained in ✍️ The letters, with the pitfalls of handwriting. Hebrew and Arabic are displayed right to left; the formulas on graves are translated (פ״נ, תנצב״ה, المرحوم…) and a small converter reads the letter-numbers (תרנ״ה = 655, i.e. 1894-1895; Armenian ՌՋԺԵ = 1915; abjad and the digits ١٣٢٠).

column2: What are 300 livres of 1780 or 1,200 francs of 1880 worth today (Old money converter)?
column3: “🪙 Old money converter” (Settings → Calendar / measures, quick search ⌘K, ⋯ of the record, record transcription): 💰 Money tab, write the sum as in the record (“12 livres 10 sous 6 deniers”, “1 200 francs”, “45 NF”, “3 écus”) and the year (“1780”, “an X”). You get the equivalent in today’s euros (≈), in bread and in days of work, and “The calculation, step by step”. From 1901, it is the INSEE price index (the same calculation as its franc-euro converter); before 1901, an order of magnitude. Exact parities: 1 livre = 20 sous = 240 deniers, 81 livres = 80 germinal francs, 1 new franc = 100 old francs, 1 € = 6.55957 F. “📋 Copy” puts the result on the clipboard.

column2: How much is an arpent, a toise, a boisseau? And the Republican calendar?
column3: “🪙 Old money converter” → 📏 Old measures: choose the region (Paris, Lyon, Brittany, Normandy, Burgundy, Provence, Lorraine, Alsace, Flanders), write “3 arpents”, “12 toises 3 pieds”, “2 setiers” (or “1.5 ha” for the reverse): the value in metres, ares or litres, the other measures of the region and the same measure elsewhere. → 📅 Republican calendar: “12 thermidor an II” or “14 July 1794”, both ways, with the day of the week and the 13 months of the year. In a record, a date in Year II is already understood (“✓ Understood: … (30 July 1794)”); “🪙 Convert” next to it opens the converter.

column2: Where do I find all my record transcriptions?
column3: Lists → Archives and sources → “📜 Record transcriptions”: each record with its thumbnail, its kind, its date, its place, its reference, the number of lines and areas, the people spotted. Search in the title, the text, the people, the place or the reference (without worrying about accents); filter by kind of record, person, place, period, state (to do, in progress, finished), with areas or linked to a record; List or Cards (with the first lines of the text); sort by date of the record. A click reopens the record; “＋ New transcription” starts by choosing the image; 🗑 deletes with “↶ Undo”. The state is chosen at the top of the tool.

column2: How do I print a beautiful large-format tree (fan, wheel, drawn tree)?
column3: Charts → “🌳 Decorative tree to print”, or Lists → Editing tools → “🌳 Decorative tree”: choose the person, the shape (fan, open fan, wheel, drawn tree with trunk, branches and foliage), the number of generations, the format (A4 to A0, posters), the style (parchment, classic, botanical, heraldic, modern, black and white) and what is written (years, dates, places, occupations, Sosa numbers, empty boxes, portraits). The tree opens in vector drawing: everything can be retouched (colours, fonts, ornaments, coat of arms), then File → Print / PDF or Export as PNG.

column2: How do I draw a town or village plan or a map of a region?
column3: In Vector drawing: Plan menu → “Plan mode”, or the 🗺️ Plan tab on the right. Choose what you are drawing in the palette (road, street, path, river, forest, field, building, church, mill, place name…), then one click per point: roads join up, rivers widen, names follow the streets. Period styles (État-Major, Napoleonic cadastre, Cassini, parchment), scale, compass rose, cartouche and automatic legend. “Base map of a place” or “Reference image” lays a map or an old plan underneath, transparent, to trace over; “Places from the database” places your places; each object can be linked to a person or a place and have its years (time slider).

column2: How do I make a hemicycle, a horseshoe or the timeline of a group’s members?
column3: Charts → “My diagrams” → “＋ Create a diagram”: 25 drawings (parliament in a hemicycle, arc, horseshoe, Westminster, circle, hall; members timeline in the Wikipedia style, timeline of lives, schedule; columns, pie chart, pyramid, flow, organisation chart, Venn, word cloud, gauges…). Type your figures, paste them from a spreadsheet, import a CSV or take them from the app (“From the app”, with “Keep up to date”). It can then go in a widget, a note, a person’s record, an investigation, the Workshop (“Link” tab) or the layout (Object → Insert a diagram).

column2: How do I create my own chart (formerly “my own statistic”)?
column3: Settings → Chart editor (formerly “Statistics editor”) → “＋ New chart” (or “＋ Create a chart” at the bottom of Charts). Start from scratch (count people, events, one of your lists… by occupation, by place, by decade, by century), from one of the app’s statistics (Surnames, First names, Places, Birth years…) redrawn your way, from one of your widgets or from an example. Eight drawings: bars, columns, pie, ring, line, area, mosaic, table. It appears in Charts → “My charts”, and can also go on the dashboard or in one of your tabs.

column2: How do I put many conditions in a chart (e.g. woodcutters within 4 km of Pernay, married, with two children)?
column3: In the Chart editor, start from one of the app’s statistics (Surnames, First names, Places…) or from a chart from scratch, then “＋ Criterion” as many times as you like: occupation, first name, surname, place, within … km of a town, between two precise dates, had an event (marriage, divorce, journey…), number of children (“2 and 2” = exactly two), number of unions, number of events of a type, age at an event, lifespan, sex, label, my ancestors. “✨ Suggest a caption” writes the sentence that sums up the criteria.

column2: How do I share a chart on a forum or with an association?
column3: Charts → My charts → your chart: “🖼️ PNG image” (to post), “📄 CSV” (the figures for a spreadsheet) or “🖨 Print / PDF”.

column2: Where do I display my chart: in Charts, on the dashboard, in a tab?
column3: In the editor, “Where to show it”: tick Charts and/or the dashboard. For one of your tabs: add it from the left column of the tab, or in Settings → Tab editor.

column2: Name and saint of the day: how do I see the people concerned?
column3: Charts → Statistics → Name and saint of the day, at the very bottom: the list of people who bear the first name of the saint of their birth or baptism day (or all of them), sortable by date, by day of the year, by name or by saint. Click on a period or a family in the tables to keep only that one.

column2: First names: the family and France, how do I see everyone?
column3: In the “In the family” column, click “＋ 12 people” (the number varies) to unfold the full list, and “Fold” to close it again.

column2: Where does an ancestor’s first name come from (godfather, grandfather, brother who died before…)?
column3: Charts → Statistics → “Passing on of first names”: for each child, the app looks for the most likely lead — their godfather or godmother (the “godfather” and “godmother” witnesses of the birth or baptism), a brother or sister who died before their birth (the first name “taken up again”), a paternal or maternal grandparent, the father or mother, an uncle or aunt, or the saint of their birth day. Each lead states its rule (“same first name as their godfather”) and a confidence level (strong, medium, weak); Jean and Jeanne, Louis and Louise count as the same first name. At the top: the transmission arrows (one line per first name, the years across; click on a circle = the record), filterable by first name, by branch and by period; then the share of children who bear their godparent’s first name, period by period. On the record, the small line “👶 First name received from…” (Identity block) has a ⋯: “That’s right”, “That’s not it”, another lead, or “Choose the person…” with the search menu; “↶ Undo” right after. Nothing is written without your click; living people and confidential records are never counted or named.

column2: How do I compare my family with French averages (age at marriage, children, mortality, signatures, occupations)?
column3: Charts → Statistics → “Your family and the history of France” (just after “Family averages”): for each period, your family’s average (orange dot) next to that of France (blue dot, “≈”): age at first marriage of men and women, children per couple, infant mortality before age 1, life expectancy, share of spouses who signed their marriage record (“signed” box of marriages), share of farming occupations. Each French figure has its source at the bottom of the page (Louis Henry and Jacques Houdaille, Yves Blayo, INED, INSEE, Maggiolo survey…); when a figure was not certain, it was not included. Filters: branch and period; a click on the number of people shows who is counted; “⤓ Export” like the other statistics. A family has few records (“⚠️ few” under 10) and babies who died are often missing from trees: the comparison should be read broadly.

column2: How do I keep a chart’s settings?
column3: At the bottom of the Charts column, “💾 Save the view”: the diagram, the person, the depth and the colours are kept in the “Saved” tab.

column2: How do I quickly find a person or a place?
column3: ⌘K: type a name, a place, a search sweep or the name of a screen.

column2: Can I ask a question in plain words?
column3: Yes: Research → Type of search → “Ask a question in plain words”, for example “Which ancestors were bakers in Lille before 1850?”. The search can then be saved.

column2: How do I search for a word in the page?
column3: ⌘F: the words found are highlighted and counted.

column2: How do I go back to the previous screen?
column3: ⌘← and ⌘→ on a Mac, Alt+← and Alt+→ on Windows and Linux. All the shortcuts: F1 key.

column2: How do I make my own list (e.g. all divorces between 1850 and 1920)?
column3: Settings → List editor → “＋ New list”: choose events, people, or rows you write yourself (stands at a fair…); combine criteria, choose the columns, add your own columns to fill in (text, menu, checkbox, link, person from the database) and labels. You can also start from a list of the app (Births, Marriages, SOSA…) or from one of your lists, show it in the Lists tab, and share it with a relative (“Share” button, then “Import a list…” on their side). Can be exported as CSV and printed.
